newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain may summon Portugal envoy on extradition row.
newsitem.headline: Spain may summon Portugal envoy on extradition row.

text.p: Spain threatened on Friday to summon the Portuguese ambassador to convey its anger at the refusal of the Lisbon high court to hand over a suspected ETA rebel.

Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said "it is very probable" the envoy would be called in after the Portuguese court on Wednesday rejected Spain's request to extradite Jose Luis Telletxea, wanted for smuggling ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) rebels and weapons across the northern border with France.

"If the Spanish courts have characterised (his actions) as a crime in Spain. The minimal professional respect would oblige the Portuguese courts to accept their Spanish colleagues' reasoning," Matutes said at a news conference.
He said Spain was considering reestablishing border checkpoints now that Telletxea was free to prevent him crossing back into Spain with impunity and committing other crimes.
Spain, for whom extradition is a highly sensitive issue, appealed for ratification of a European extradition treaty.

"If the treaty on extradition had been approved, it is possible we would not find ourselves in the situation we are in today with Portugal," government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez told reporters after the weekly cabinet meeting.

"For this reason it is important to continue insisting in the area of extradition and to understand this is something we Spaniards need because the unity of all European Union countries against terrorists benefits us," he added.
Spain hopes it will be easier to prosecute wanted ETA rebels captured outside its borders once the 15 EU members ratify an extradition convention signed in Dublin last September.
Once ratified, countries will no longer be able to refuse extradition on grounds the offence was political.
Portugal had agreed with Spain the two countries would implement the EU extradition pact as soon as their parliaments had ratified it without waiting for other member countries.
Portuguese newspapers said the latest ruling was based on a lack of evidence to back Spain's case.
But Spanish Justice Minister Margarita Mariscal said on Thursday the case was solid and blamed the decision on lack of coordination among Portugal's judicial bodies.

"We will wait until we receive the ruling and it is very probable the Portuguese ambassador will be summoned to express to him our concern, our unhappiness, and obviously to demand measures from him," Matutes said.

Portuguese Justice Minister Jose Vera Jardim told Reuters in an interview on Friday he did not yet know the full reasons for the court's decision but said it was final. He denied it meant Portugal was a safe haven for ETA guerrillas.

A group of left-wing Portuguese politicians and intellectuals, including members of the ruling Socialist Party, recently circulated a petition against Telletxea's extradition, warning he could face torture if returned to Spain.
A similar diplomatic row erupted between Madrid and Brussels last year when a Belgian court ruled against extraditing a couple suspected of collaborating in an ETA attack.
The Spanish cabinet also decided on Friday to ask France to extradite Jose Luis Urrusolo Sistiaga, the presumed number three in ETA who was detained last month.
Spain will also repeat requests to France to hand over two other suspected ETA guerrillas, Julian "Pototo" Atxurra Egurola and Carmen Guisasola Solozabal.
